name: Concealer (for men)

lead: Concealer is a thick, highly pigmented makeup used on small areas, most often to mask under-eye dark circles, spots, redness and scars. It comes as liquid, cream, stick, pencil and cream-to-powder, and is blended in with fingers, a brush or a sponge.

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a quick, low-cost way to reduce the look of eye bags and uneven skin, and also as something some men feel self-conscious about buying or wearing. Research on concealer itself is sparse, and nearly all of it is not specific to men.

paras: Concealer works optically: its pigment sits on top of the skin and blocks or neutralises the darker or redder tone beneath it. Makeup guides describe yellow or peach tones for dark circles, and green for redness such as pimples or rosacea, and recommend a shade one or two steps lighter than the skin for brightening [1].

Concealer is a cosmetic and is generally sold without prescription. Some products contain ingredients such as fragrance, mineral oil, dimethicone or talc [1]. A 2021 questionnaire study of 539 Korean adults examined links between cosmetic use and acne [4]. Because it only masks, it does not change the underlying cause of dark circles or blemishes.

lead: Concealer is a cosmetic used to mask skin imperfections such as dark under-eye circles, blemishes and hyperpigmentation. It is similar to foundation but more heavily pigmented, usually applied in small amounts and then blended with a brush, sponge or fingertips [1]. It can be worn over or under foundation, or on its own [1][2].

Products come in several forms: liquid, stick, cream, pencil and cream-to-powder, each with different coverage and finish [1]. Colour theory is part of its use. Makeup references describe yellow-toned concealers for dark circles, green or blue tones to counteract red areas, and purple-tinted products for sallow complexions [1].

In looksmaxxing forums, concealer is described mostly in the context of under-eye bags and dark circles, and members discuss how to use it discreetly. Published research on concealer as a product is limited, and no study in the sources reviewed tests it in men specifically.
infobox: Dark circles, blemishes, redness, hyperpigmentation, scars [1][2]
Temporary cosmetic cover; does not treat the cause

paras: Wikipedia describes liquid concealer, sold in tubes or vials with satin, radiant or matte finishes, as the most popular form and suited to most skin types. Stick concealer is thicker and gives high coverage for small areas and touch-ups. Cream concealer is thick and opaque, often applied with a brush and also used for birthmarks. Pencil concealer is creamy or wax-based for small spots, and cream-to-powder compacts give a matte finish [1].

An AI-generated encyclopedia entry adds that liquid concealers are generally lightweight and buildable, creams more emollient and suited to dry skin, and sticks portable but potentially prone to sliding on oily skin without powder; this entry should be treated with caution because it is machine-written [2].

People often choose a shade one or two steps lighter than their skin, according to Wikipedia. Yellow-toned concealers are used for dark circles, green and blue tones counteract redness from pimples, broken veins or rosacea, and purple tints are said to brighten sallow complexions [1]. The same principle of neutralising a colour with its complement underlies the 'colour corrector' products sold in green and peach tones for redness and under-eye darkness [2].

Wikipedia dates the first commercially available concealer to Max Factor's Erace, launched in 1954 [1]. An AI-generated encyclopedia entry also credits Lydia O'Leary's Covermark, introduced in 1930 for scars and birthmarks, as an earlier camouflage product, and traces later developments such as colour-correcting concealers in the 1980s and wider shade ranges after 2017 [2]. The 1930 claim is not corroborated by the sources otherwise reviewed here.

Wikipedia lists common ingredients, which include castor seed oil, dimethicone, talc, mineral oil and fragrance [1]. A 2021 questionnaire study of 539 Korean individuals examined the relationship between acne and the use of cosmetics [3]. A laboratory study published in 2020 formulated an anti-acne concealer containing cinnamon oil and tested its activity against acne-associated bacteria in vitro [4].

On looksmax.org, one poster describes concealer as the best 'looksmax' for people of colour because, they say, many have naturally persistent under-eye darkness, and posts before-and-after photos to show the difference [5]. Other threads concern social aspects: members ask how to buy and keep concealer without family noticing [6], and one member recounts being noticed wearing it by a parent [7]. A looksmax.org guide thread is titled as advice on hiding dark circles without looking as if makeup is worn [8].
Surveys or trials on male concealer use are not in the sources reviewed.
No studies found on concealer for men or for dark circles specifically.

Related published work includes a 2021 study on the safety and efficacy of a cosmetic camouflaging agent for post-procedural bruising [9], a 2021 study of the clinical correlates of periocular dark-circle severity [10], and a 1988 article on the need for and use of corrective cosmetics [11].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org concealer is treated as an inexpensive cover for dark circles, alongside some discussion of stigma around men wearing makeup [5][6][7].

claims.claim: Concealer is one of the most effective cheap 'looksmaxes', especially for people with permanent dark eye bags.
Concealer can be applied so that it does not look like makeup.
Men wearing concealer face social stigma and conceal their use.
